title: France and the limits of liberalism
gist: Noah Smith argues France's riots amid surging yields and default-insurance costs reveal limits of left-liberal welfarism, Keynesian demand management and tolerant immigration policy, since pensions and taxes are already maxed out and benefits ratchet upward.

insights.claim: France's long-term interest rates are surging and the cost of insuring against French sovereign default has risen even more abruptly, as investors doubt the government will raise taxes or cut spending to repay debt.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: French sovereign spreads and CDS are a stress gauge for euro-area debt risk.

insights.claim: Paul Krugman argues France is on a fiscally unsustainable path, with high debt, large deficits without emergency, aging-driven pension costs and a retirement age of only 62 in 2023 whose planned rise to 64 is frozen until after next year's election.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Pension rigidity is the core driver of French default perception.

insights.claim: France's government takes a larger share of GDP than almost any other rich country, more than Sweden or Denmark, and its taxes as a share of GDP exceed any other rich country, leaving little room for either austerity route.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Limited fiscal levers raise tail risk of a French debt crisis spilling over the euro area.

insights.claim: France's earlier tax experiments failed: the wealth tax raised only a few billion euros (about 1% of tax revenue) while at least 10,000 wealthy people left, and the 75% supertax raised just 160 million euros in 2014 before repeal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Capital flight within the EU makes taxing the rich a weak option for deficit repair.

insights.claim: Riot demands for more school, pension and benefit spending raise bond yields, which increases interest costs and makes the spending the protesters want harder to afford.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Unrest worsens the bond-market feedback loop, a negative for French assets.

insights.claim: Smith argues the French riots show the limits of European left-liberal welfarism, with social benefits acting as a one-way ratchet in which even mild austerity triggers riots.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political feasibility of austerity is a key variable for developed-market fiscal risk.
insights.quote: social benefits seem to be a one-way ratchet

insights.claim: Keynesian stimulus requires austerity during booms, which is politically very hard; during the 2010s euro crisis France neither cut nor stimulated, with spending and debt sailing on unperturbed while Germany did austerity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect deficit bias in democracies; supports higher long-term term premia.

insights.claim: Krugman wrote in 2011 that deficits would matter once out of the liquidity trap, so Smith says Hanno Lustig's charge of inconsistency is somewhat unfair.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Context for the debate on whether deficit hawkishness is a reversal.

insights.claim: As disorder began, Marine Le Pen's election chances on Polymarket rose while those of left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon did not budge, suggesting voters gravitate toward whoever promises to stop immigration.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Prediction-market odds for the French election are shifting toward the right, a political risk factor for France.

insights.claim: Smith says it is not obvious immigrants disproportionately drive these riots, since rioters appear racially mixed, but the French public increasingly blames migrants, and that left-liberal immigration approaches do not work equally for all countries.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Perception, not facts, drives voting shifts toward anti-immigration parties.
